section_summary: This section comprises U.S. State Department despatches, memoranda, cross-reference sheets, and press clippings from late 1933 to 1936 documenting communist and radical developments in Japan and adjacent regions. American diplomats, including Ambassador Joseph C. Grew and State Department specialist Eugene H. Dooman, report that orthodox communism in Japan is waning due to extensive police suppression, counter-propaganda by Christian and conservative groups, and public recantations by imprisoned leaders. At the same time, social and economic unrest among farmers and laborers is increasingly co-opted by reactionary military and fascist factions advocating national socialism under imperial sovereignty. Accompanying records track related communist investigations, educational purges, and anti-Soviet propaganda in Korea, Manchukuo, the Soviet Union, and Turkey.

subfiles.about: Concluding section of a diplomatic despatch evaluating recent communist developments, intellectual and judicial arrests, and public criticism of futile police suppression in Japan.
subfiles.summary: This concluding segment of a Tokyo Embassy despatch reports that the Japanese Communist Party's regeneration was crippled following the Omori bank robbery. It highlights the shocking arrests of prominent intellectuals including Dr. Hajime Kawakami and Professor Kinnosuke Otsuka, as well as Tokyo Local Court judge Susumu Ozaki and judicial officer Chosuke Sakamoto. Analyzing press sentiment, it quotes an Asahi editorial arguing that police oppression fails to extinguish radicalism and urges freedom of speech and thought as a safety valve. The despatch concludes that radicalism in Japan reflects social unrest rather than a true revolutionary communist program.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch on Communist Developments and Judicial Arrests

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing a memorandum on the growth of communism in Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: This State Department document file note cross-references memorandum 893.01 Manchuria/920 dated June 25, 1933, prepared by Laurence E. Salisbury of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs. It notes that an increase of communism in Manchukuo is believed to be preparing the way for an eventual government under Japanese communism.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Memorandum on Manchukuo Communism (894.00B/53)

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum analyzing Tokyo Despatch No. 596 and contrasting the prospects of communism versus national socialism in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Eugene H. Dooman of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs reviews Tokyo Despatch No. 596, comparing Walter Washington's recent observations with Laurence Salisbury's earlier reports from 1926 to 1932. The memorandum examines the decline of communism among university students and notes that reactionary military and fascist societies have stolen communist thunder by championing the downtrodden. Dooman argues that while Japan's communal tradition makes it receptive to socialized concepts, communism would require abolishing the imperial dynasty; therefore, should capitalism fail, Japan will turn to national socialism rather than communism.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 596 Regarding Communism in Japan

subfiles.about: Comprehensive diplomatic report detailing the decline of communism in Japan, Christian counter-campaigns, police roundups, and the ascendance of reactionary nationalism.
subfiles.summary: Tokyo Despatch No. 596 provides an exhaustive assessment of communism in Japan, concluding that the movement is on the decline despite sensational press coverage of police roundups. It analyzes student radicalism and explains how educational campaigns organized by Christian bodies such as the YMCA successfully diminished communist influence in universities. The report explains that rural peasants and factory workers are increasingly drawn to patriotic reactionary and fascist groups that borrow socialist economic tenets while venerating the Emperor. It also reviews the arrests of Zenkyo unionists, the heavy representation of Koreans in radical labor activities, and the controversial prison recantations ('reforms') of communist leaders.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 596: 'Communism in Japan'

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing Tokyo Despatch No. 607 regarding police arrests of 1,696 suspected radicals.
subfiles.summary: This document file note cross-references Tokyo Despatch No. 607 (Periodic Report No. 72), dated December 11, 1933, from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew. It records that between February and November 1933, 1,696 persons were arrested by Japanese police on charges of being radicals.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 607 on Radical Arrests (894.00B/55)

subfiles.about: Extract from Periodic Report No. 72 covering the lifting of a press ban on Zenkyo arrests and cumulative communist arrest statistics from 1928 to 1933.
subfiles.summary: This extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 607 (Periodic Report No. 72) reports the lifting of a long-standing press ban on November 20, 1933, disclosing that 1,696 members of the Zenkyo labor council had been arrested for attempting to overthrow the government and establish a proletarian dictatorship. It reproduces statistics from The Japan Times showing that over 29,000 communist sympathizers were handled by the Tokyo District Court procurator between 1928 and October 1933. The report notes with particular interest that three district court judges and five clerks were among those held guilty in preliminary examinations.
subfiles.title: Extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 607 (Periodic Report No. 72): Section on Communism

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum discussing an interview with former communist leader Katsumaro Akamatsu on the rise of nationalism in Japanese labor.
subfiles.summary: Eugene H. Dooman of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs analyzes Tokyo Despatch No. 628, reiterating his assessment that Japan's communal orientation makes it receptive to national socialism rather than communism. He focuses on the ideological shift expressed by former communist leader Katsumaro Akamatsu, who contrasts Western individualistic liberalism with the Oriental worldview that regards the Japanese Empire as a single great organic family life.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 628 Regarding Views of Former Communist Leader

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch transmitting a Japan Advertiser press interview with former communist labor leader Katsumaro Akamatsu.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits a newspaper clipping from The Japan Advertiser of December 19, 1933, reporting an interview with Katsumaro Akamatsu. Grew notes that Akamatsu, a favorite pupil of the late Dr. Sakuzo Yoshino, was once a prominent communist leader and that his new nationalistic stance reflects the current trajectory of radical thought among the Japanese working class.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 628: Transmitting Newspaper Interview of Former Communist Leader

subfiles.about: Newspaper clipping interview with Katsumaro Akamatsu explaining why international Marxism has failed in Japan and why trade unions have turned nationalistic.
subfiles.summary: This newspaper article reports an interview with Katsumaro Akamatsu, head of the Kokumin Kyokai and the Japan Mailmen's Union, who argues that over 95 percent of Japanese labor unions have embraced nationalism because internationalism has proven to be a dismal failure. Akamatsu maintains that labor interests run parallel to national industrial prosperity and asserts that the exclusion of Japanese labor by American unions demonstrates the bankruptcy of international labor solidarity. He contrasts Western liberal individualism with the Oriental philosophy of the state as a sacred imperial family, arguing that industrial control belongs to the sovereign Emperor rather than capital or labor.
subfiles.title: Clipping from The Japan Advertiser: 'Japanese Laborers Turn Nationalistic'

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing Tokyo Despatch No. 656 regarding communist arrests and indictments in Korea.
subfiles.summary: This document file note cross-references Despatch No. 656 (Periodic Report No. 73), dated January 9, 1934, from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew. It records that twenty-nine communists were arrested in Korea, with twenty-two indicted under the Peace Preservation Law and seven cautioned and dismissed.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 656 on Communist Arrests in Korea (894.00B/57)

subfiles.about: Extract from Periodic Report No. 73 detailing the arrest of radical schoolteachers in Korea and primary school educators in Osaka.
subfiles.summary: This extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 656 reports the lifting of a press ban in Korea revealing the arrest of twenty-nine radicals, twenty-two of whom were indicted under the Peace Preservation Law for using reverse interpretations of school textbooks to instill racial prejudice and communism in students. The report adds that police in Osaka detained five primary school teachers for establishing an institute of radical education in conjunction with the Proletarian Artists' League.
subfiles.title: Extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 656 (Periodic Report No. 73): Note on Communism

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing a Moscow despatch regarding the growth of communism in Japan.
subfiles.summary: This document file note cross-references Despatch No. 24, dated April 16, 1934, from Ambassador William C. Bullitt in Moscow (filed under 761.94/734). It indexes information regarding the growth of communism in Japan.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Moscow Despatch No. 24 on Growth of Communism in Japan (894.00B/58)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note referencing a report on General Mazaki's speech before the Japanese League for the Struggle Against Communism in Tokyo.
keywords: Japanese League for the Struggle Against Communism
subfiles.summary: This document file note cross-references Despatch No. 327, dated July 14, 1934, from Ambassador Robert P. Skinner in Turkey (filed under 711.61/503). It indexes an account of an address delivered by General Jinzaburo Mazaki at a meeting of the Japanese League for the Struggle Against Communism held in Tokyo on March 26, 1934.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Istanbul Despatch No. 327 on Mazaki Report (894.00B/59)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indexing a Harbin despatch regarding Kwantung Army anti-Soviet propaganda and a lecture on war prospects between Japan and the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: This document file note cross-references Despatch No. 424, dated October 8, 1936, from Vice Consul Robert L. LaMont at Harbin (filed under 761.94/933). It notes Kwantung Army anti-Soviet propaganda and encloses a copy of Despatch No. 269 to Peiping transmitting a Ukrainian lecture delivered in Harbin on the prospects of war between Japan and the Soviets.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Harbin Despatch No. 424 on Kwantung Army Anti-Soviet Propaganda (894.00B/60)
